records.name: Anastazas
records.facts_used: The Senn–Salys Lithuanian–German dictionary marks Anastazas as a short form of Anastazijus, the Lithuanian form of Latin Anastasius. Anastasius is the Latinized Greek Anastasios, “resurrection”, from anastasis, composed of ana “up” and stasis “standing”. Antanas Salys’s 1964 name calendar, reprinted in his collected writings in 1983, lists Anastazas on 22 January with the short forms Anastas and Nastas. This dates a published calendar entry; it does not identify the first Lithuanian bearer or the time the name was formed.

Salys’s 1964 name calendar places Džiugas on 9 May, not on 22 January as in this project’s calendar. records.name: Vincentas
records.facts_used: The Senn–Salys dictionary marks Vincentas as a personal name corresponding to German Vinzenz and lists Vincas as its short form. The family goes back to the Roman cognomen Vincentius, derived from Latin vinco, “to conquer”. Antanas Salys’s 1964 calendar places Vincentas (Vincas) on 22 January. In an article on Lithuanian surnames, Salys notes that sixteenth-century court records written in Ruthenian often used Vencko for Vincentas. Such chancery forms entered everyday speech and, through patronymics, later produced surnames such as Venckus. This is a documented historical name form, not the first use of Vincentas.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: The sixteenth-century form is Salys’s general statement about court records, not an independently inspected archive or first bearer. Checked location: Dictionary PDF 278 / printed 263 (Vincentas PN Vinzenz; Vincas KF); calendar PDF 301 / printed 286; Mūsų pavardės PDF 36 / printed 21 (16th-century Ruthenian court acts Vencko = Vincentas); curated BTN Vincent opening. Original PDF pages were visually read where used; catalogue transcriptions remain attributed.

records.name: Luuli
records.facts_used: Edgar Rajandi discusses Luuli within the history of Luule, which he calls an original Estonian feminine name. He notes that when Luule was first proposed, the word luule did not yet have its present meaning, “poetry”; that modern sense should therefore not be read back as the name’s original meaning. According to Rajandi, Mats Tõnisson’s almanacs of 1896–1903 promoted the form Luuli, and O. Kallas proposed Luule anew in 1910; the first Luules were entered in birth registers in 1910/1911. These dates concern documented calendar proposals, not the first Estonian bearer of Luuli.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
